# Patent Disclosure

> **Title**: Declarative Profile Driven Polymorphic Adaptation for Canonical Unikernel Images  
> **Invention ID**: invention-20260623-163539  
> **Company**: Red Hat  
> **Generated**: 2026-06-23 16:37:48

---

# Problem Statement

Right now, deploying unikernels across different platforms, tenants, or environments means building and maintaining a separate image for each one. Customers running heterogeneous infrastructure with different API conventions, communication protocols, resource models, and operational tooling force providers to produce distinct variants for every environment. Every variant needs its own compilation, testing, security audit, and patch cycle, and at scale this becomes a real problem. Serving hundreds of customers across cloud, edge, and on-premises environments produces a variant matrix that nobody can reasonably manage. There's also a divergence risk: security patches or feature updates may reach some builds before others, creating inconsistent security postures across the deployment fleet. No existing mechanism lets a single unikernel image dynamically conform its external behavior to diverse client environments while keeping a unified internal execution core.

---

# Technical Implementation

We embed an adaptation layer within a single canonical unikernel image. At initialization, this layer consumes a declarative adaptation profile, cryptographically verifies its authenticity, and reshapes the unikernel's exposed APIs, communication protocols, resource models, and runtime behaviors to match the target environment. Once activation finishes, the system reclaims dormant capability modules by unmapping their memory pages and sealing the remaining address space, so only the selected personality survives in the running instance.

The canonical image ships with a superset of capabilities: multiple protocol handlers, API surface variants, configuration schema interpreters, and resource model adapters. All compiled in, all dormant until activated. Alongside these capabilities sits what we call the adaptation engine, a lightweight initialization subsystem that reads the externally supplied profile and decides which capabilities come alive for a given deployment.

At boot time, the adaptation profile arrives through whatever platform mechanism is available: a mounted volume, a cloud metadata service, or an injected environment block. It describes the tenant's expected interfaces (REST, gRPC, or a proprietary RPC format), protocol conventions (mTLS settings, header propagation rules, authentication token formats), resource models (memory accounting style, CPU share semantics, storage abstractions), and operational behaviors (health check endpoints, metrics emission format, log structure). The profile contains no code. It selects and parameterizes capabilities already present in the canonical image.

Before acting on any profile content, the engine verifies the profile cryptographically. Each profile carries a digital signature produced by the profile registry's signing key. The adaptation engine holds the corresponding public key, either embedded at image build time or retrieved from a trusted attestation service, and validates the signature against the profile payload. If the signature is absent, invalid, or produced by an unrecognized key, the unikernel refuses to initialize and emits a tamper detection event to the platform's audit log. This prevents an attacker who gains write access to the profile delivery mechanism from injecting a crafted profile that activates an unintended combination of capabilities.

Initialization proceeds as a transactional activation sequence with a ledger recording each module's state. The engine activates the appropriate protocol listeners and binds them to the network stack, tearing down any the profile does not reference. It wires the selected API surface into the unikernel's internal service layer, which stays the same regardless of external personality. Resource model configuration follows so the unikernel reports usage in whatever format the surrounding orchestrator expects. Last to come up is the operational personality: health probe endpoints, the expected metrics format (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or a vendor format), and the structured logging schema. If any module in this sequence fails, the engine consults the ledger and rolls back every previously activated module in reverse order, returning each to its dormant state, then fails closed with a structured error identifying the failure point and stage. A unikernel running with an incomplete personality could expose unexpected behavior or create security gaps, so partial activation is never allowed.

Once all selected modules are active, a capability reclamation pass begins. The engine walks through every unselected module and unmaps the memory pages backing those dormant code paths and data structures. On platforms that support it, the engine marks reclaimed address ranges as inaccessible using hardware memory protection (page table manipulation on x86, or stage 2 translation restrictions under a hypervisor). Dormant modules are not merely inactive after this step. They are physically unreachable from the running address space. An exploit in an active module cannot pivot to dormant code because that code simply no longer resides in addressable memory. The adaptation engine then seals its own reclamation logic through the same mechanism, rendering itself inert for the rest of the instance's lifetime. What you end up with is a true minimal footprint, only the code paths required by the active personality remain, nothing more.

Outside the unikernel, a profile registry service manages adaptation profile lifecycle. Operators author profiles for each deployment context, store them in the registry, and associate them with scheduling metadata so the orchestrator injects the right profile automatically when launching instances. The registry validates that a profile only references capabilities present in the canonical image version being deployed, preventing mismatches that would surface as silent boot failures. It also serves as the signing authority for profiles, and operators can rotate signing keys through its key management interface while configuring the canonical image to trust multiple keys during rotation windows. Because every deployment starts from the same compiled binary, vulnerability scanning, attestation, and supply chain verification happen exactly once. No dynamic code loading, JIT compilation, or plugin injection ever occurs.

    PR -->|"Signed profile injected\nat boot time"| SV

    subgraph Canonical["Canonical Unikernel Image (single binary)"]

        SV -->|"Verified profile"| AE
        AE["Adaptation Engine\n(transactional activation + reclamation)"]

            P2["Auth Modules\nmTLS | OIDC | Bearer"]
            P3["Resource Adapters\ncgroup-v2 | millicore | virtio"]

        end

        AE -->|"2. Unmap dormant\nmodule memory pages"| Reclaim["Memory Reclamation\n(page unmap + seal)"]

```

The diagram traces the flow from profile injection through signature verification, transactional activation of selected capability modules, and memory reclamation of dormant ones. Activated modules wire into an internal service layer that stays the same across all deployments. The same canonical image produces entirely different external personalities depending on which profile was injected.

# Problem Statement

Right now, deploying unikernels across different platforms, tenants, or environments means building and maintaining a separate image for each one. Customers running heterogeneous infrastructure with different API conventions, communication protocols, resource models, and operational tooling force providers to produce distinct variants for every environment. Every variant needs its own compilation, testing, security audit, and patch cycle, and at scale this becomes a real problem. Serving hundreds of customers across cloud, edge, and on-premises environments produces a variant matrix that nobody can reasonably manage. There's also a divergence risk: security patches or feature updates may reach some builds before others, creating inconsistent security postures across the deployment fleet. No existing mechanism lets a single unikernel image dynamically conform its external behavior to diverse client environments while keeping a unified internal execution core.

# Technical Implementation

We embed an adaptation layer within a single canonical unikernel image. At initialization, this layer consumes a declarative adaptation profile, cryptographically verifies its authenticity, and reshapes the unikernel's exposed APIs, communication protocols, resource models, and runtime behaviors to match the target environment. Once activation finishes, the system reclaims dormant capability modules by unmapping their memory pages and sealing the remaining address space, so only the selected personality survives in the running instance.

The canonical image ships with a superset of capabilities: multiple protocol handlers, API surface variants, configuration schema interpreters, and resource model adapters. All compiled in, all dormant until activated. Alongside these capabilities sits what we call the adaptation engine, a lightweight initialization subsystem that reads the externally supplied profile and decides which capabilities come alive for a given deployment.

At boot time, the adaptation profile arrives through whatever platform mechanism is available: a mounted volume, a cloud metadata service, or an injected environment block. It describes the tenant's expected interfaces (REST, gRPC, or a proprietary RPC format), protocol conventions (mTLS settings, header propagation rules, authentication token formats), resource models (memory accounting style, CPU share semantics, storage abstractions), and operational behaviors (health check endpoints, metrics emission format, log structure). The profile contains no code. It selects and parameterizes capabilities already present in the canonical image.

Before acting on any profile content, the engine verifies the profile cryptographically. Each profile carries a digital signature produced by the profile registry's signing key. The adaptation engine holds the corresponding public key, either embedded at image build time or retrieved from a trusted attestation service, and validates the signature against the profile payload. If the signature is absent, invalid, or produced by an unrecognized key, the unikernel refuses to initialize and emits a tamper detection event to the platform's audit log. This prevents an attacker who gains write access to the profile delivery mechanism from injecting a crafted profile that activates an unintended combination of capabilities.

Initialization proceeds as a transactional activation sequence with a ledger recording each module's state. The engine activates the appropriate protocol listeners and binds them to the network stack, tearing down any the profile does not reference. It wires the selected API surface into the unikernel's internal service layer, which stays the same regardless of external personality. Resource model configuration follows so the unikernel reports usage in whatever format the surrounding orchestrator expects. Last to come up is the operational personality: health probe endpoints, the expected metrics format (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or a vendor format), and the structured logging schema. If any module in this sequence fails, the engine consults the ledger and rolls back every previously activated module in reverse order, returning each to its dormant state, then fails closed with a structured error identifying the failure point and stage. A unikernel running with an incomplete personality could expose unexpected behavior or create security gaps, so partial activation is never allowed.

Once all selected modules are active, a capability reclamation pass begins. The engine walks through every unselected module and unmaps the memory pages backing those dormant code paths and data structures. On platforms that support it, the engine marks reclaimed address ranges as inaccessible using hardware memory protection (page table manipulation on x86, or stage 2 translation restrictions under a hypervisor). Dormant modules are not merely inactive after this step. They are physically unreachable from the running address space. An exploit in an active module cannot pivot to dormant code because that code simply no longer resides in addressable memory. The adaptation engine then seals its own reclamation logic through the same mechanism, rendering itself inert for the rest of the instance's lifetime. What you end up with is a true minimal footprint, only the code paths required by the active personality remain, nothing more.

Outside the unikernel, a profile registry service manages adaptation profile lifecycle. Operators author profiles for each deployment context, store them in the registry, and associate them with scheduling metadata so the orchestrator injects the right profile automatically when launching instances. The registry validates that a profile only references capabilities present in the canonical image version being deployed, preventing mismatches that would surface as silent boot failures. # Problem Statement

Right now, deploying unikernels across different platforms, tenants, or environments means building and maintaining a separate image for each one. Customers running heterogeneous infrastructure with different API conventions, communication protocols, resource models, and operational tooling force providers to produce distinct variants for every environment. Every variant needs its own compilation, testing, security audit, and patch cycle, and at scale this becomes a real problem. Serving hundreds of customers across cloud, edge, and on-premises environments produces a variant matrix that nobody can reasonably manage. There's also a divergence risk: security patches or feature updates may reach some builds before others, creating inconsistent security postures across the deployment fleet. No existing mechanism lets a single unikernel image dynamically conform its external behavior to diverse client environments while keeping a unified internal execution core.

---

# Technical Implementation

We embed an adaptation layer within a single canonical unikernel image. At initialization, this layer consumes a declarative adaptation profile, cryptographically verifies its authenticity, and reshapes the unikernel's exposed APIs, communication protocols, resource models, and runtime behaviors to match the target environment. Once activation finishes, the system reclaims dormant capability modules by unmapping their memory pages and sealing the remaining address space, so only the selected personality survives in the running instance.

The canonical image ships with a superset of capabilities: multiple protocol handlers, API surface variants, configuration schema interpreters, and resource model adapters. All compiled in, all dormant until activated. Alongside these capabilities sits what we call the adaptation engine, a lightweight initialization subsystem that reads the externally supplied profile and decides which capabilities come alive for a given deployment.

At boot time, the adaptation profile arrives through whatever platform mechanism is available: a mounted volume, a cloud metadata service, or an injected environment block. It describes the tenant's expected interfaces (REST, gRPC, or a proprietary RPC format), protocol conventions (mTLS settings, header propagation rules, authentication token formats), resource models (memory accounting style, CPU share semantics, storage abstractions), and operational behaviors (health check endpoints, metrics emission format, log structure). The profile contains no code. It selects and parameterizes capabilities already present in the canonical image.

Before acting on any profile content, the engine verifies the profile cryptographically. Each profile carries a digital signature produced by the profile registry's signing key. The adaptation engine holds the corresponding public key, either embedded at image build time or retrieved from a trusted attestation service, and validates the signature against the profile payload. If the signature is absent, invalid, or produced by an unrecognized key, the unikernel refuses to initialize and emits a tamper detection event to the platform's audit log. This prevents an attacker who gains write access to the profile delivery mechanism from injecting a crafted profile that activates an unintended combination of capabilities.

Initialization proceeds as a transactional activation sequence with a ledger recording each module's state. The engine activates the appropriate protocol listeners and binds them to the network stack, tearing down any the profile does not reference. It wires the selected API surface into the unikernel's internal service layer, which stays the same regardless of external personality. Resource model configuration follows so the unikernel reports usage in whatever format the surrounding orchestrator expects. Last to come up is the operational personality: health probe endpoints, the expected metrics format (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or a vendor format), and the structured logging schema. If any module in this sequence fails, the engine consults the ledger and rolls back every previously activated module in reverse order, returning each to its dormant state, then fails closed with a structured error identifying the failure point and stage. A unikernel running with an incomplete personality could expose unexpected behavior or create security gaps, so partial activation is never allowed.

Once all selected modules are active, a capability reclamation pass begins. What you end up with is a true minimal footprint, only the code paths required by the active personality remain, nothing more.

Outside the unikernel, a profile registry service manages adaptation profile lifecycle. It also serves as the signing authority for profiles, and operators can rotate signing keys through its key management interface while configuring the canonical image to trust multiple keys during rotation windows. Because every deployment starts from the same compiled binary, vulnerability scanning, attestation, and supply chain verification happen exactly once. No dynamic code loading, JIT compilation, or plugin injection ever occurs.
